Dear Steve

               
I’m glad you agreed to collaborate with me. Since we spoke I have indeed been hard at work, and I’ve already made some rather interesting discoveries.

               
There are three Pages on Facebook that correspond to the plot of the novel. The pages date from August of 2012, and there is considerable activity between 21/08 and 29/08, after which the story seems to end. It appears that someone set up these pages, one for Vincent, one for Jadee, one for Davison, and then allowed them to interact with real people, before writing up the results in the form of a novel. Of course, this raises all sorts of awkward questions about who, if anyone, is the real author here.

               
I am convinced that there is something sinister about this book. I’m having nightmares. I’m sure that there is some hidden message coded into the work, and that I have absorbed it, subconsciously, but am unable to spell it out. When I was working on ch.3, the scene in which the phone rings and Vincent speaks to The Voice for the first time, my own phone started ringing, right on cue, and when I answered it there was no one there. Even as I write this, the hairs on my arms are on end.

               
I scanned my paper copy of the pages and converted them to Microsoft Word format so we can work on them easily. I’ve taken a rather antitraditional approach in my annotations which I hope you will find engaging. I have attached the first few chapters to this email. I’ve also saved them in a Google folder and invited you to edit. This will help us to keep track of the changes we are making:

               

                  

               
               
Can we use this file from now on, please?

               
Also, in my footnotes, I’m referring to your original piece as the ‘Courier Strand’ because that’s the font used in the file. The numbered chapters I’m referring to as the ‘Palatino Strand’ for the same reason.

               
Best,

               
Ike

one
         
         
I’m sitting in an internet café in a hotel, looking at a photo of a dead girl. The photo arrived a few seconds ago: an email attachment from my guy. I call my guy The Voice because that’s all he is to me. He might be an ally, might be a kibitzer. He’s been giving me instructions for the last day or so. But that doesn’t mean anything. He might have been giving me instructions for months. I don’t remember, and it isn’t important anyway.

         
The girl in the photo is Emily. And I’m beginning to wonder, is that why I came here? To find out who killed her? All I know is that I woke up in an empty apartment and ever since then The Voice has been calling me on the phone, emailing me, leaving me clues.8

         
Emily’s neck is twisted to the left. One eye is open. The other eye is obscured by the gelatinous mass that spills from a jagged crack in her skull. The brain-matter I’m looking at reminds me of something I’ve seen before – something like mixing tomato ketchup into scrambled eggs as a child. The face is so badly disfigured that were it not for the signature denim hotpants and Dr Martens I doubt I would recognise Emily at all.

         
There’s a girl in the internet café, sitting opposite me. There are a couple of tourists in here too, tapping away on their keyboards. I’m sitting with my back against the wall, so no one can see the picture I’m looking at and no one can see me seeing it either.9 I stand up and look around for the bathroom. I go into one of the stalls and throw up, and then return to the computer and reread the email. 

         

            
You considered opening the door, didn’t you?

            
I know more about you than you may think. I know things about you that you don’t even know yourself. In fact, I’ve got so much shit on you that I could completely destroy you. But I want to help you. I’m going to give you two choices.

            
1: Leave. I’ve booked you a flight back to Manchester. It’s EasyFly America: confirmation #41229191514.10 I will never contact you again. Your flight leaves at midday tomorrow.

            
2: Stay here and await further instructions.

            
Before you make your decision, open the attachment I’ve included with this email.

         
         
I think about the bedroom at the apartment. One of the first things The Voice said when he called me after I woke up was, Don’t open the door. Don’t look in the bedroom. Hell is waiting for you. I took his advice.

         
The Internet is crawling along very slowly, and I picture a fatally wounded animal hauling its wrecked body to the hard shoulder of a motorway. As I picture this, I also picture the word ‘fracture’. I pick some crumbs from between the keys on the keyboard and consider ordering a drink, but they don’t serve booze here. It’s what Americans refer to as a Dry Bar.11 I look at my hands. They’re shaking. I might have a hangover, or perhaps I’m nervous about something. It’s difficult to know whether I have a hangover, because I can’t remember whether I’ve had a drink. It’s difficult to know whether I’m nervous, because I can’t remember whether I have anything to be nervous about.

         
I’m finding it hard to concentrate because of the pain in my back. I think it started when I woke up in the apartment, but it could’ve been before that. It radiates from my lower west side, near my kidneys, or at least near the spot where I imagine my kidneys to be.12 It lingers, spreading its heat through my abdomen like the after-ache of a swift kick to the bollocks, and it’s definitely getting worse. I’m clasping my left hand against my ribcage, applying pressure like I’m trying to prevent an alien from bursting out of me. Colour-wise, the sensation is an intense orange or red. 

         
The machine tells me that I’m signed in as Vincent Ballone, and that it is customising my settings. It tells me it’ll take seven minutes to do this, and I have twenty-three minutes of time remaining. There’s a clock on the bottom right-hand side of the screen and it’s counting down to the cut-off point while I imagine the mournful tick, tock, tick of a time bomb. When the page finally reloads, I email The Voice and ask him to get in touch and tell me where to meet him. After I hit send, I lift myself off my seat and reach in my back pocket. I run my thumb along the tattered edge of the picture I always keep there – a passport-style photo of Emily that used to be stuck to our fridge. I tease it free and lay it face down on the desk. The back of the photo was once a brilliant white, but now it’s got the faint sepia hue of a jaundiced eyeball. I want to turn the picture over to look at it, but I just can’t.13 I put it back in my pocket and stare at the image on the computer screen instead; it’s horrifically vivid and strangely sexual. The lukewarm throb of pain waxes and wanes in my back and I feel like I’ve swallowed a handful of stones. 

         
I switch off the computer without shutting it down and stagger out of the café into the lobby. The girl at the reception desk has a noisy expression like interference on a TV screen and eyes that flicker like they’re being tuned in. I feel drunk. For all I know, I am drunk. The room spins around me like a roulette wheel. The pain is unbearable now. There is a washing-up bowl full of dirty dishwater in my guts and there is grit in my veins: tiny shards of glass with precisely sharpened edges designed to cut me up from the inside. I make it to the bathroom again, but the stall I so gratefully threw up in earlier now displays an Out of Order sign and it feels like a personal attack.14 I run to the basins, put both hands on the porcelain, and throw up, retching gobs of green and red bile into the plughole, spattering the glass with it, shaking violently as long spiderwebs of snot and vomit trail from both my nostrils. I watch myself puke in the mirror. My performance is disgusting but very theatrical.15 I cough horridly, wondering whether my guttural hackings will get the attention of the girl in the café next door.

         
My eyes and nostrils are streaming with the acid burn and my throat is on fire. The pain in my kidney has shifted and it feels as though something is stuck in my chest now, somewhere unpinpointable, like the origin of an orgasm. I cough and retch, trying to get it out. One final surge erupts from deep within me like slurry from a burst sewer pipe, and then I’m done. I wipe my mouth. I gob a bit and wipe my nose.

         
There’s something black in the sink. Something other than the blood and bile and chunks of partially digested crisps. Something synthetic. Something unhuman. I look closer.

         
It is a key from a computer keyboard.

         

            
8 See ch.3.

            
9 Interestingly, David Foster Wallace remarked that metafiction is ‘nothing more than a poignant hybrid of its theoretical foe, realism: if realism called it like it saw it, metafiction simply called it as it saw itself seeing itself see it’ (See Christopher R. Beha, ‘Reconstruction’, London Review of Books, 33:9). In other words, ‘metafiction’ and ‘realism’ are not mutually exclusive terms. Similar to ‘magic realism’, it is possible to achieve a kind of metafictional realism in the sense that metafictional elements of the plot can be blended into the consciousness of the protagonists so as not to break the realist frame. Intriguing point!

            
10 EasyFly America is not a currently trading organisation.

            
11 The use of capital letters here could be significant. The Dry Bar, Manchester, was a music venue located in the heart of the city’s Northern Quarter, on Oldham Street. Note that the denouement at the end of the Courier strand comes after a meeting in the same district. Well spotted… It seems the links between this narrative and my original story run a lot deeper than I first imagined…

            
12 A three-sided pun. Lower west side = the bottom left of the back, the area of New York City in which the mysterious apartment is located, and a stylistic nod towards Martin Amis’s novel Money.

            
13 It occurs to me that the presence of the photo, and the fact that the protagonist carries it with him at all times in his back pocket, directly mirrors the scratch card motif found in the Courier strand.

            
Could it be that the photograph and the scratch card are both metaphors for the same thing, and, if so, what? I suggest that both the photograph and the scratch card are representative of the multiverse theory, which states that as soon as there is the potential for an object to exist in any state, the universe occupied by that particular object splits into a series of parallel universes, the number of which indicates the number of possible states that the object may potentially have. Scientists such as Werner Heisenberg have argued that quantum mechanics cannot render an accurate description of objective reality because the very act of measuring something causes it to assume only one of these possible states – this is referred to as the Copenhagen Interpretation. This idea is explored by means of a discussion of Schrödinger’s cat paradox which accounts for the notion that nothing ‘exists’ until it is measured. In Schrödinger’s theoretical experiment, a cat is placed into a sealed, opaque chamber, along with a device containing a vial of hydrocyanic acid. If a single atom of the acid decays then a hammer will be tripped which will break the vial and kill the cat. Since it is impossible for the observer to know whether or not an atom of the substance has decayed, it is also impossible to know, without breaking open the box, whether the cat is alive or dead. According to quantum law, the cat is both dead and alive. It is only when the box is broken open that the various possible ‘states’ of the cat are reduced to a single state, and the cat becomes either dead or alive. Similarly, it could be the case that Vincent sees Emily as neither alive nor dead, but both at the same time, in the same way as the second-person narrator in the counter-narrative sees himself as simultaneously rich and poor. I don’t suppose we’ll ever know for certain whether this observation is correct. The links seem clear to me too, but there’s no way to ascertain the true intentions and motivations of whoever added these chapters. Unless we can trace them and ask, of course.

            
14 Is ‘Out of Order’ a reference to the work’s complex chronology? Perhaps!

            
15 This, I argue, is one of many examples of the metafictional devices subtly embedded in the text. Vincent’s assertion that his performance is theatrical draws readers’ attention to the fact that he is not only an actor but also self-aware. Not sure about this. It makes sense, of course, but it seems a bit too convenient and too clumsy.
